tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I wonder where he is.
I wonder where is he.
Could you tell me what time the train leaves?
Could you tell me what time does the train leave?
She asked whether the bakery was still open.
tactical_explanations:
**A) I wonder where he is.**

After wonder, the embedded clause must keep statement order: where + subject + verb. Here that gives where he is, which matches the pattern exactly. The outer I wonder already asks; the inner clause does not need question order of its own.

Accept the line: after wonder, where he is keeps calm statement order.
**B) I wonder where is he.**

The string where is he inverts the verb and subject, which belongs only in a direct question. After I wonder you need where he is. Cover I wonder and you immediately hear a stand-alone quiz question — that is the scar.

**Trap:** where is he looks like ordinary spoken curiosity, but it is direct-question order jammed into an embed.

Mark it wrong and prefer "I wonder where he is."
**C) Could you tell me what time the train leaves?**

The polite frame Could you tell me… embeds what time the train leaves with subject before verb. No does appears inside the clause, which is exactly what an indirect question wants. The outer Could you… supplies the interrogative force for the whole sentence.

That works — tell me embeds what time the train leaves with subject before verb.
**D) Could you tell me what time does the train leave?**

does the train leave is direct-question word order jammed into an indirect question. Any do/does/did that jumps before the subject after tell me is almost always wrong. The frame already asks; the embed should stay flat.

**Trap:** Adding does after tell me feels like extra clarity, but it recreates a direct question.

That fails here — rewrite as "Could you tell me what time the train leaves?"
**E) She asked whether the bakery was still open.**

whether correctly opens a yes/no embed and keeps statement order: the bakery was still open. There is no were-fronting after whether. Yes/no embeds follow the same calm subject–verb rule as wh-embeds.

Keep this: whether the bakery was still open never flips were before the subject.
tasks.solution_overview:
You are judging whether each sentence embeds its question the English way — as a calm statement clause after wonder, tell me, or ask — rather than as a stand-alone question.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Indirect questions keep statement word order after the wh-word or after whether/if. The outer softener (I wonder, Could you tell me) already carries the questioning force. What fails is stray do-support or a swapped auxiliary–subject pair smuggled into the embed.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Cover the outer frame and read only the clause after where / what time / whether. If that clause still looks like a quiz show question (where is he?, does the train…?), mark it false. If it reads like ordinary news (where he is, the train leaves, the bakery was), mark it true.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Do you know if the library has opened yet?
Do you know if has the library opened yet?
Please explain why the soup burned.
Please explain why did the soup burn.
They could not decide which route was safer.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Do you know if the library has opened yet?**

if embeds a yes/no clause with normal order: the library has opened yet. has stays after the library, not before it. The outer Do you know… is already the direct question; the inner clause stays flat.

This is sound: if the library has opened keeps the auxiliary after the subject.
**B) Do you know if has the library opened yet?**

if has the library… wrongly inverts the auxiliary into the embedded clause. Keep if the library has…. Treat any has/is/will sitting right after if as a red flag.

**Trap:** Auxiliary fronting after if copies a yes/no question and looks almost right in exams.

Reject this near-miss; the clean version is "Do you know if the library has opened yet?"
**C) Please explain why the soup burned.**

why the soup burned is statement order after explain; no auxiliary is needed. The past verb burned already carries tense, so there is nowhere for did to go. Explain why… invites a reason clause, not a second question.

Hold onto this: why the soup burned needs no did inside the reason clause.
**D) Please explain why did the soup burn.**

why did the soup burn mirrors a direct question. The embedding verb already carries the interrogative force, so drop did. If you can strip the outer Please explain and still have a complete quiz question, the embed is inverted.

**Trap:** did-support after why is the classic classroom leftover inside embeds.

Flag it false and go with "Please explain why the soup burned."
**E) They could not decide which route was safer.**

which route was safer keeps subject–verb order inside the embedded choice. route is the subject of was; nothing is fronted. which + noun + verb is the calm pattern you want.

Leave it as written: which route was safer reads like ordinary prose order.
tasks.solution_overview:
These items sit after know, explain, and decide — verbs that swallow a full subordinate question without letting it keep direct-question gymnastics.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Focus on if/whether and on wh-clauses (why, which). Correct items keep the subject before the finite verb. Wrong ones smuggle has…? or did…? inversion into the subordinate clause.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Find the embed opener (if, why, which) and check the next two words. If an auxiliary has already jumped ahead of the subject, the item is false. If you hear a quiet subject–verb pair, the item is true.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The question is how the team will respond.
The question is how will the team respond?
I am not sure what caused the blackout.
I am not sure what did cause the blackout.
She asked whether were the tickets still valid.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The question is how the team will respond.**

After The question is, how the team will respond uses statement order: subject team before will. The noun-phrase frame does not license inversion. Read it aloud without rising question intonation inside the how-clause — it should sound like news.

Trust the order here: how the team will respond sits flat under The question is.
**B) The question is how will the team respond?**

how will the team respond? is a direct question glued onto The question is. You need subject, then modal: how the team will respond. The trailing question mark is another giveaway that someone forgot the clause was embedded.

**Trap:** Modal inversion after how looks like a tidy question mark fix, but embeds forbid it.

Mark it wrong and prefer "The question is how the team will respond."
**C) I am not sure what caused the blackout.**

what is the subject of caused, so no do-support is required or allowed. Subject wh-clauses already have their actor in the wh-word. what caused the blackout is the whole story.

That pairing is right — subject what caused needs no do-support.
**D) I am not sure what did cause the blackout.**

what did cause forces unnecessary do-support into an embedded subject question. Use what caused, not what did cause. Save did for object questions that need tense support in direct speech — not for subject who/what embeds.

**Trap:** did after subject what feels emphatic or 'complete,' but it is wrong in this embed.

That tense choice fails — rewrite as "I am not sure what caused the blackout."
**E) She asked whether were the tickets still valid.**

whether were the tickets… inverts were and the subject after whether. whether never takes the yes/no flip that stand-alone Were the tickets…? uses. Slide were back after tickets.

**Trap:** were-fronting after whether is a near-miss copy of a direct yes/no question.

Reject this; the clean embed is "whether the tickets were still valid."
tasks.solution_overview:
Noun-phrase frames (The question is…, I am not sure…) still demand embedded statement order — and subject questions refuse fake did.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Two classic traps: modal inversion after how (will the team…) and unnecessary do-support in a subject question (what did cause…). A third trap is were-fronting after whether.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask whether the wh-word is the subject of the next verb. If it is, you never need did. Otherwise check that any modal or be-form sits after its subject, not before. Correct embeds read like calm statements parked inside a larger sentence.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: They could not decide which option was it safer.
I'd like to know when the guests arrive.
I'd like to know when do the guests arrive.
Can you remind me where the spare keys are kept?
Can you remind me where are the spare keys kept?
tactical_explanations:
**A) They could not decide which option was it safer.**

Extra pronoun it after was breaks the clause; which option was safer is already complete. Never park a dummy it after the verb in an embedded which-clause. The option is the subject — you do not need a second subject.

**Trap:** Adding it after was feels like filling a slot, but the which-phrase already filled the subject.

Drop the dummy it and rewrite as "which option was safer."
**B) I'd like to know when the guests arrive.**

when the guests arrive keeps subject–verb order after I'd like to know. Softeners do not change the embedded word-order rule. arrive sits after guests, exactly where a statement puts it.

Accept the line: when the guests arrive keeps subject then verb after I'd like to know.
**C) I'd like to know when do the guests arrive.**

when do the guests arrive inserts do-support as if the clause were a direct question. The outer I'd like to know already asks; the inner clause should not. Delete do and keep statement order.

**Trap:** do after when is a plausible softener leftover from classroom drills.

That fails — strip do and prefer "I'd like to know when the guests arrive."
**D) Can you remind me where the spare keys are kept?**

where the spare keys are kept is passive statement order inside a polite question. are stays after the subject keys. Passives still obey the same subject-before-finite-verb rule.

Keep this: where the spare keys are kept stays passive and uninverted.
**E) Can you remind me where are the spare keys kept?**

where are the spare keys… flips are before the subject inside the embed. where + subject + are/is is the pattern; where + are + subject is the scar. The softener Can you remind me does not license that flip.

**Trap:** Be-fronting after where is the most common location-embed trap.

Mark it wrong and prefer "Can you remind me where the spare keys are kept?"
highlights: where the spare keys are kept
tasks.solution_overview:
Polite frames such as I'd like to know and Can you remind me feel soft, but they still forbid inversion inside the embedded clause — and they reject an extra dummy it.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Dummy it after which… was is a common repair that actually breaks the clause. Separately, do-support and be-fronting after when/where are direct-question leftovers.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

First check whether the which-clause already has a subject (which option…); if it does, add nothing. Then strip the softener and see whether the remaining clause still sounds like a quiz question. If it does, mark false; if it sounds like a statement, mark true.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Nobody could say who had locked the gate.
Nobody could say who had the gate been locked by.
We need to establish whether the courier can arrive by noon.
We need to establish whether can the courier arrive by noon.
Tell me how much the tickets will cost.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Nobody could say who had locked the gate.**

who is the subject of had locked, so statement order is natural and correct. Nobody could say… merely frames a subject question. Subject who/what never invert with the verb.

This is sound: subject who had locked the gate never needs a flip.
**B) Nobody could say who had the gate been locked by.**

who had the gate been… forces awkward inversion and a stranded by that belongs in a rewritten object question. Prefer who had locked… or the formal by whom the gate had been locked. If the embed starts shoving auxiliaries past the subject just to save a passive, rewrite instead.

**Trap:** Passive who-embeds often look formal while quietly breaking subject–auxiliary order.

Reject that awkward passive; prefer "who had locked the gate."
**C) We need to establish whether the courier can arrive by noon.**

whether the courier can arrive… keeps modal can after the subject. That is the textbook whether + subject + modal + verb pattern. The outer We need to establish… does not license a yes/no flip inside.

That works — whether the courier can arrive parks can after the subject.
**D) We need to establish whether can the courier arrive by noon.**

whether can the courier… is direct yes/no inversion after whether. Never put the modal before the subject in an embedded clause. Slide can back after courier.

**Trap:** Modal fronting after whether copies Can the courier…? almost exactly.

Flag it false and rewrite as "whether the courier can arrive by noon."
**E) Tell me how much the tickets will cost.**

how much the tickets will cost is statement order after Tell me. will stays after tickets, not before how much. Degree how much/how many phrases behave like other wh-embeds.

Hold onto this: how much the tickets will cost keeps will after tickets.
highlights: how much the tickets will cost
tasks.solution_overview:
Subject who stays simple; modal whether-clauses and how much-clauses keep the modal after the subject. Awkward passive inversions are a separate red flag.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

who as subject needs no flip and no stranded-by rewrite that drags the auxiliary forward. whether + subject + can… is fine; whether can the… is not. how much… will… similarly refuses will-fronting.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Locate who / whether / how much and check what immediately follows. If a modal or auxiliary has jumped ahead of its subject, reject the item. Prefer the clean subject who + past participle pattern when both active and awkward passive are offered.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Tell me how much will the tickets cost.
The note does not say how long the delay lasted.
The note does not say how long did the delay last.
Parents asked what the school intended to do next.
Parents asked what did the school intend to do next.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Tell me how much will the tickets cost.**

how much will the tickets cost inverts will and the subject after Tell me. The same how much phrase is fine with statement order: how much the tickets will cost. That contrast is intentional across these tasks.

**Trap:** will-fronting after how much is a near-miss of the Direct How much will…? shape.

Mark it wrong and prefer "Tell me how much the tickets will cost."
**B) The note does not say how long the delay lasted.**

how long the delay lasted keeps statement order after say. lasted is a plain past verb after its subject; no auxiliary is waiting to front. Duration how long-clauses follow the same calm pattern as why-clauses.

Accept the line: how long the delay lasted is flat statement order after say.
**C) The note does not say how long did the delay last.**

how long did the delay last smuggles do-support into the embed. If the clause would be a perfect stand-alone question, it is too inverted for this frame. Delete did and keep the past verb after the subject.

**Trap:** did after how long feels natural from oral drills, but embeds ban it here.

That fails here — rewrite as "how long the delay lasted."
**D) Parents asked what the school intended to do next.**

what the school intended… is an object-wh clause with subject before verb. school sits before intended; what is the object of intended. After asked, keep what + subject + verb.

Keep this: what the school intended puts the subject before the past verb.
**E) Parents asked what did the school intend to do next.**

what did the school intend… is a direct question sitting inside asked. Drop did and keep intended after school. Object what often tempts learners into full question order — resist it in embeds.

**Trap:** Object what + did is a very plausible direct-question transfer.

Reject this near-miss; the clean version is "what the school intended to do next."
highlights: how much will the tickets cost
how long did the delay last
tasks.solution_overview:
how much, how long, and object what-clauses all crash when will or did jumps before the subject. Correct embeds keep the finite verb after the subject noun.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Tell me / say / asked open the frame; the damage lives inside the subordinate clause. will-fronting after how much and did-support after how long or what are the usual scars.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Read from the wh-word to the verb and ask whether anything has skipped ahead of the subject. If will or did appears before the noun that should be the subject, mark false. If the subject sits in its ordinary slot, mark true.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I can't remember where I put my passport.
I can't remember where did I put my passport.
Have you found out whether the museum opens on Mondays?
Have you found out whether does the museum open on Mondays?
She wondered why everyone was whispering.
tactical_explanations:
**A) I can't remember where I put my passport.**

where I put my passport is statement order after remember. I is the subject; put is the past verb — nothing is inverted. Memory verbs still take embedded statement order.

Leave it as written: where I put my passport is memory-clause statement order.
**B) I can't remember where did I put my passport.**

where did I put… is direct-question do-support inside an embedded clause. can't remember does not license a second, inverted question. Use where I put….

**Trap:** did after where is the default oral memory-question shape learners paste into embeds.

That fails — drop did and prefer "where I put my passport."
**C) Have you found out whether the museum opens on Mondays?**

whether the museum opens… keeps opens after the subject. No does appears, and none is needed. Perfect for a yes/no fact-check after find out.

This is sound: whether the museum opens never invents does after whether.
**D) Have you found out whether does the museum open on Mondays?**

whether does the museum open… invents do-support after whether. does belongs in Does the museum open…? as a stand-alone question, not here. Use whether the museum opens….

**Trap:** does after whether looks like careful tense marking but recreates a direct question.

Mark it wrong and prefer "whether the museum opens on Mondays."
**E) She wondered why everyone was whispering.**

why everyone was whispering keeps was after the subject. wonder why… wants a reason clause, not a flipped be-question. The progressive was whispering stays intact after everyone.

Trust the order: why everyone was whispering keeps was after the subject.
tasks.solution_overview:
Memory, discovery, and wonder verbs — remember, find out, wonder — all embed statement order. Stand-alone question shapes after where or whether do not belong.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

did-fronting after where and does-fronting after whether are the scrapes. Correct why / where / whether clauses place the subject before was, opens, or the past verb.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Cover the matrix verb and judge only the subordinate string. If it still sounds like a quiz (where did I…?, whether does the…?), reject it. If it sounds like a report (where I put…, whether the museum opens…), accept it.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She wondered why was everyone whispering.
Let me know which bus you are taking.
Let me know which bus are you taking.
We still don't know who broke the window.
We still don't know who did break the window.
tactical_explanations:
**A) She wondered why was everyone whispering.**

why was everyone… inverts was before the subject after wondered. The twin with why everyone was whispering is the correct shape. wonder why… never takes be-fronting inside the reason clause.

**Trap:** Be-inversion after why is a classic wonder-clause near-miss.

Reject this be-fronting; rewrite as "why everyone was whispering."
**B) Let me know which bus you are taking.**

which bus you are taking keeps you before are. which + noun + subject + verb is the embedded choice pattern. Let me know simply softens the request; it does not invert the clause.

Accept the line: which bus you are taking keeps you before are.
**C) Let me know which bus are you taking.**

which bus are you taking flips are before you inside the embed. If you can hear Are you taking…? after stripping the frame, the item is false. Use which bus you are taking.

**Trap:** are-fronting after which + noun copies the Direct Which bus are you…? drill.

Flag it false and go with "which bus you are taking."
**D) We still don't know who broke the window.**

who broke the window is a clean subject question with no do-support. who is the agent; broke is the past verb. Subject who + past verb needs no did.

Keep this: subject who broke the window needs no did.
**E) We still don't know who did break the window.**

who did break adds unnecessary emphatic or wrong do to a subject question. Emphatic did can appear in speech for contrast, but it is not the neutral embed pattern tested here. Use who broke, not who did break.

**Trap:** Emphatic did after subject who looks confident and still fails the exam pattern.

That fails — prefer the neutral "who broke the window."
tasks.solution_overview:
This set pairs be-inversion after why with are-fronting after which, then finishes on subject who without fake did.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

why was everyone… and which bus are you… both mark direct-question order. Subject who broke… stays simple: never who did break in this embed.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

After wonder / let me know / don't know, check whether was/are/did has jumped ahead of its subject. For who, ask whether who is the subject of a plain past verb — if yes, reject any added did. Statement order wins every time.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I'm curious how often she practises the piano.
I'm curious how often does she practise the piano.
Can anyone say where the nearest pharmacy is?
Can anyone say where is the nearest pharmacy?
They asked if we had packed enough water.
tactical_explanations:
**A) I'm curious how often she practises the piano.**

how often she practises… keeps subject–verb order after curious. Frequency phrases do not change the embedded rule. practises sits after she, as in ordinary prose.

**Tip:** Frequency wh-phrases still take statement order.

That works: how often she practises still takes statement order after curious.
**B) I'm curious how often does she practise the piano.**

how often does she practise… inserts do-support as in a direct question. I'm curious already softens the ask; does is leftover from classroom drills. Use how often she practises….

**Trap:** does after how often is a near-miss of How often does she…?

Mark it wrong and prefer "how often she practises the piano."
**C) Can anyone say where the nearest pharmacy is?**

where the nearest pharmacy is places is after the subject noun phrase. That is the classic location embed. Can anyone say… is the outer question; the where-clause stays flat.

Hold onto this: where the nearest pharmacy is parks is after the noun phrase.
**D) Can anyone say where is the nearest pharmacy?**

where is the nearest pharmacy flips is before the subject inside say. This is the same signature contrast you meet with wonder where… throughout the topic. Use where the nearest pharmacy is.

**Trap:** is-fronting after where remains the signature location trap at every difficulty.

Reject this near-miss; the clean version is "where the nearest pharmacy is."
**E) They asked if we had packed enough water.**

if we had packed… is a yes/no embed with statement order. had stays after we; the past perfect is intact. if/whether + subject + verb — never invert.

This is sound: if we had packed keeps had after we.
tasks.solution_overview:
Frequency how often, location where…is, and if-clauses all stay calm: subject then verb, no fronted auxiliary.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

how often fails when does jumps before she. where…is fails when is jumps before the nearest pharmacy. if-clauses fail when any auxiliary front-runs the subject.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Treat how often and where like any other wh-embed: cover curious / say / asked and judge the rest. Accept only the versions that could be rewritten as statements without moving words around. Reject any that still need quiz-show intonation.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: They asked if had we packed enough water.
Nobody knows how many people will show up.
Nobody knows how many people will show up will.
Please check whether the oven has preheated.
Please check whether has the oven preheated.
tactical_explanations:
**A) They asked if had we packed enough water.**

if had we packed… inverts had before we after asked. The true twin if we had packed… shows the correct order. Auxiliaries do not front after if.

**Trap:** had-fronting after if is a close twin of Had we packed…?

That fails here — rewrite as "if we had packed enough water."
**B) Nobody knows how many people will show up.**

how many people will show up keeps will after the subject people. how many + noun + will + verb is the calm degree pattern. Nobody knows… frames it without turning it into a direct question.

Accept the line: how many people will show up leaves will after people.
**C) Nobody knows how many people will show up will.**

Extra will at the end is garbled; the clause is already complete after show up. Stop at how many people will show up. A trailing echo of will usually means someone rewrote the clause twice and forgot to delete.

Mark it wrong and stop at "how many people will show up" — drop the trailing will.
**D) Please check whether the oven has preheated.**

whether the oven has preheated keeps has after the subject. whether + subject + auxiliary + participle is the perfect yes/no embed. Please check softens the request without inverting the clause.

Keep this: whether the oven has preheated leaves has after oven.
**E) Please check whether has the oven preheated.**

whether has the oven… flips has before the subject. Same scar as if had we… — auxiliaries do not front after whether/if. Use whether the oven has….

**Trap:** has-fronting after whether is a textbook near-miss yes/no embed error.

Flag it false and prefer "whether the oven has preheated."
highlights: how many people will show up
tasks.solution_overview:
Watch for had-fronting after if, has-fronting after whether, and a garbled extra will at the end of an otherwise finished how many-clause.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

The yes/no embeds invert when auxiliaries leapfrog the subject. how many people will show up is fine once; trailing will is noise, not grammar.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

After if or whether, demand subject then auxiliary. For how many, accept a single will after the subject noun and stop when the clause is complete. Anything that restacks will or has before the subject fails.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The guide explained how the bridge had been built.
The guide explained how had the bridge been built.
I need to find out whose jacket this is.
I need to find out whose is this jacket.
Did anyone mention when the concert starts?
tactical_explanations:
**A) The guide explained how the bridge had been built.**

how the bridge had been built keeps passive statement order after explained. had stays after bridge; the passive stack been built follows. Passive embeds still place the first auxiliary after the subject.

**Tip:** Passive embeds still place had after the subject.

Leave it as written: how the bridge had been built keeps had after the subject.
**B) The guide explained how had the bridge been built.**

how had the bridge been… inverts had into direct-question order. Explained how… does not invite a quiz-show flip of the auxiliary. Use how the bridge had been built.

**Trap:** Passive stacks tempt had-fronting that looks especially 'complete' in exams.

Reject this flip; rewrite as "how the bridge had been built."
**C) I need to find out whose jacket this is.**

whose jacket this is keeps this before is. whose + noun + subject + be is the ownership embed. find out frames the question without fronting is.

**Tip:** whose + noun + subject + be.

That works — whose jacket this is keeps this before is.
**D) I need to find out whose is this jacket.**

whose is this jacket flips is before this inside find out. Moving whose alone and fronting be is the classroom direct-question habit. Use whose jacket this is.

**Trap:** whose is this… looks polished and still breaks embed order.

Mark it wrong and prefer "whose jacket this is."
**E) Did anyone mention when the concert starts?**

when the concert starts is statement order after mention; the outer Did anyone… is the only direct question. Outer inversion does not license inner inversion. starts sits after concert, as a fact report would.

**Tip:** Outer inversion does not license inner inversion.

Trust the outer question alone: when the concert starts stays flat inside.
highlights: how the bridge had been built
tasks.solution_overview:
Passive how-clauses and whose…is patterns both fail when the auxiliary precedes the subject. A direct outer question never licenses inversion inside the embed.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

how had the bridge… and whose is this jacket move had/is ahead of their subjects. when the concert starts after mention stays statement-ordered even though Did anyone… opens the sentence.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Separate outer inversion from inner order. Only the outer frame may flip; the subordinate clause must still read as a statement. For whose, keep the noun with whose and put the subject before be.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Did anyone mention when does the concert start?
We're trying to work out what the noise is coming from.
We're trying to work out what is the noise coming from.
He refused to say whether he would join us later.
He refused to say whether would he join us later.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Did anyone mention when does the concert start?**

when does the concert start inserts do-support inside the embedded clause. Did anyone mention… already asked; the embed should not ask again. Use when the concert starts.

**Trap:** does inside when after a direct Did anyone… is a double-ask near-miss.

That fails — strip does and prefer "when the concert starts."
**B) We're trying to work out what the noise is coming from.**
